You have two ropes; each takes exactly 60 minutes to burn completely, but neither burns at a steady rate. Using only these two ropes and matches, how do you measure exactly 45 minutes?
choices: Cut each rope in half, light all four pieces at once, and stop when the first piece burns out.

Light rope A at both ends and rope B at one end at the same time. When rope A finishes burning (30 minutes), light the second end of rope B -- it will finish 15 minutes later, for a total of 45 minutes.
Light both ropes at both ends at the same time; they will both burn out together in exactly 45 minutes.
Light both ropes at one end each; stop timing when rope A finishes, since that marks 45 minutes.

Two people each bet their necktie on whose is cheaper, without knowing either value. Each reasons: 'If I lose, I lose my tie's value; if I win, I gain a tie worth more than mine — so this game favors me.' Both reason identically. Does this argument actually mean the game favors both players?
choices: No — the reasoning is flawed; by symmetry the game favors neither player
Yes — the game truly favors both, which is why it's called a paradox
No — it favors whoever proposed the bet
No — it favors whoever has the more expensive tie
